Case Study 01 — Original Design Analysis

Session length as a hidden retention risk in VALORANT

Design Proposal — not shipped work VALORANT Player Retention & Time Economics

The Observation

A ranked VALORANT match typically runs 30–40 minutes, sometimes considerably longer with overtime. In that same block of free time, I can usually finish two or three matches of Marvel Rivals or Overwatch, each running roughly 10–20 minutes — and queue times factor into that gap too, not just the matches themselves. All four are games I actively play at a high level, so this isn't a preference difference; it's a scheduling one.

The Problem

As free time gets scarcer — a job, a shifting schedule, less predictable evenings — players don't necessarily stop enjoying a game. They start optimizing for what reliably fits. A game with a large, semi-unpredictable minimum time commitment is the one that gets skipped when a window doesn't clearly fit it, even if it's still someone's preferred game. That's not a complaint about ranked's format on competitive-integrity grounds — it's a retention risk hiding in plain sight: play frequency can quietly drift toward shorter-session competitors over time, and that drift compounds long before anyone would describe themselves as having "quit" VALORANT.

Solutions I Considered

  • Introduce a shorter ranked format — fewer rounds, no overtime. Rejected: ranked's round-based economy — buy phases, saving, force-buys, comeback potential — is core to what the mode is actually testing. Shortening it to solve a scheduling problem breaks the economy the format depends on, which is a much bigger cost than the retention risk it would fix.
  • Surface expected match-length data before queueing — recent average duration, overtime frequency for that queue. Partially already true: Riot shows a static per-mode estimate today (e.g., "~40 min" for Competitive). The gap is that it's generic, not dynamic — it doesn't reflect current overtime rates or a player's own recent match lengths, so it doesn't actually tell you what tonight's queue is likely to cost you.
  • A game mode playlist / queue selection covering shorter formats that already exist — Swiftplay, Spike Rush, Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Escalation, and Skirmish (2v2/3v3, gunplay-only). Let players choose upfront which of these they're willing to accept and queue them into whichever pops first, instead of Ranked. Chosen: doesn't touch ranked's identity or economy at all, and puts the choice in the player's hands instead of an opaque backend decision.

Why This One

A playlist selector fixes the actual mismatch — time available versus time required — without touching what ranked is for or how its economy works. Letting a time-constrained player choose Spike Rush or Swiftplay instead of losing the session entirely keeps them inside the game, playing something Riot already built, on a night ranked was never going to fit.

The Trade-off I'd Watch For

Actively promoting more of these modes isn't free: every additional queue a player can land in splits the matchmaking population further. More queues can mean smaller pools per queue, longer waits at off-peak hours, and worse match quality in the queues being pushed — the exact problem this proposal is trying to avoid, just moved to a different mode.

Refining the Fix: A Multi-Mode Playlist Selector

Rather than an algorithm silently deciding which short mode to route someone into, give players a playlist-style selector: check off which shorter modes you and your group are willing to accept — Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Escalation, Spike Rush, Skirmish — and get placed into whichever one pops first. That keeps the choice with the player instead of an opaque backend decision, and it naturally respects each mode's own queue restrictions: a duo can select Skirmish 2v2, but a group of four would see it grayed out, since parties above a mode's cap aren't eligible for it. The same selector works solo or with friends — it just filters the list to whatever your current party size actually qualifies for. Checking multiple modes pools the population behind one search instead of splitting it across five separate queues, so accepting more options gets you into a game faster.

How I'd Validate It

  • A/B test: track week-over-week return rate for players who get routed to a suggested short-form mode during a detected tight window, versus a control group given no suggestion.
  • Check whether ranked queue frequency actually drops for time-constrained segments, or simply reallocates within the same session — the real goal is retained playtime, not necessarily retained ranked queues specifically.
  • Compare wait times for a pooled playlist selection against each mode's existing standalone queue, to confirm checking more modes actually reduces time-to-match rather than just redistributing it.
Case Study 02 — Team Capstone

Card Mage: designing a boss that stays threatening as the player gets stronger

Unity / C# Team of 4+ — my scope: enemy & boss design

Enemy Behavior Design

Before the boss, the base enemies needed to teach players how to read threats and use the environment. Each type was built to demand a different response, not just a different sprite:

  • Red skulls fire a continuous stream of projectiles — a sustained-pressure threat that punishes standing still, closer to a zone-denial tool.
  • Blue skulls fire a single large, slower shot — a read-and-dodge threat that rewards reacting to a clear telegraph rather than constant movement.
  • Ghosts hit the player on contact, but pass through walls and terrain — they can't be lost by breaking line of sight, so the counterplay is distance and timing, not positioning.
  • Slimes also hit on contact, but are blocked by walls like the player is — against slimes, terrain is a real tool; against ghosts, it isn't.

That last distinction was the one I cared about most: two enemies with the same basic attack (melee contact) that ask for opposite spatial decisions. A player who learns to duck behind cover from a slime and tries the same thing against a ghost gets punished for it — which is intentional pressure to keep reading enemies individually rather than pattern-matching to "stay near walls."

That variety wasn't the starting design. Early builds used a single swarming enemy type driven by real pathtracing AI, and it swung hard in both directions during testing: without effective pathfinding it was too passive to threaten anyone, and once the pathtracing actually worked, that same enemy swarmed players with no readable pattern to react to — overwhelming instead of challenging. Splitting difficulty across distinct, learnable enemy behaviors (rather than one aggressive AI doing everything) is what came out of that failure.

Early build — a single enemy type swarming the player, before difficulty was split across behaviors

The Problem

Our deck-based combat game let players build increasingly powerful decks over a run. A boss designed around early-run power levels would trivialize by the end; one balanced around late-run power would feel impossible early. I owned enemy behavior and the final boss encounter, and needed a fight that stayed tense regardless of when a player reached it.

Solutions I Considered

  • A single fixed boss pattern with stats scaled to average expected player power. Simple to build, but guarantees the fight feels wrong for anyone above or below the "average" run — which was most players.
  • A multi-phase boss where later phases introduce new mechanics (not just bigger numbers) tied to progression, keeping the challenge qualitative rather than purely statistical. Chosen: a new mechanic can't be brute-forced by raw deck power the way a stat check can, so the fight stays interesting across skill and power levels.
  • Difficulty options selectable by the player before the fight. Would've worked, but shifts the design problem onto the player instead of solving it — and was out of scope for the team's remaining time.

Difficulty Scaling Across the Run

The Knight isn't a one-time gate — clearing it once wasn't the end of how it was used. On a later level, the same boss returns as a palette-swapped, tougher variant that layers its earlier attacks together rather than replacing them: the ring projectiles, the area-denial orb, and swarming skull enemies all show up in the same encounter instead of one at a time. It's a cheap way (visually, a recolor) to get a second real difficulty spike out of one boss's moveset, by changing how its pieces combine rather than building a new fight from scratch.

What Changed After Playtesting

Several phase transitions were reworked mid-project when testers described the fight as frustrating rather than tense — a distinction I treated as a design bug, not a player-skill problem. I also diagnosed and fixed hit-registration and projectile issues that were quietly distorting the intended difficulty curve: an enemy that reads as "unfair" because a hitbox is wrong isn't a difficulty problem on paper, but it's absolutely a design problem to the person playing it.

Case Study 03 — Team Project

Break Room: scoping interaction design for a medium with no playbook

Unity / Oculus Quest 2 Team of 4 (2 CS / 2 Psychology)

The Premise

Break Room's core idea was catharsis: give players the stress relief of smashing objects with none of the real-world cost, cleanup, or consequences. That premise is what made the interaction and destruction systems the actual heart of the project — if grabbing and breaking things didn't feel satisfying, nothing else about the game mattered.

The Problem

Of our four-person team, only two of us had CS backgrounds — myself and one other student handled all of the engineering, while our two psychology teammates focused on the player-facing side: comfort, reactions, and whether an interaction actually felt convincing. VR interaction and destruction don't have decades of flat-screen precedent to lean on either, so with two engineers building systems that had no established "feel" to copy, our initial technical approach for destruction and interaction turned out to exceed what we could realistically finish and polish in the time we had.

How the Systems Fit Together

The two systems I owned had to share state on every object: something had to be trackable as both "currently held" and "destructible" at the same time, which is where a lot of the underestimated complexity actually lived.

Simplified system diagram — not from the original project files.

The Decision

With two engineers and no existing pattern to lean on for either system, pushing forward on the original scope risked shipping both systems broken rather than one system working well. We scoped the interaction and destruction mechanics down to a version two people could actually build, test, and polish — while our psychology teammates kept testing how it felt to grab and break things in headset, since a system that's technically correct but doesn't feel convincing in VR fails just as hard as one that's buggy. It was a real-time lesson in scoping ambition against team capability, not just time: a smaller mechanic that fully works beats a larger one that's half-implemented.
